title: Bitter Creek
subtitle: Ransom County, Wyoming Territory, April to June 1886

listing.title: Bitter Creek 🐂
listing.blurb: Wyoming Territory, spring 1886. A cattle company with Laramie money and a dead list against the homesteaders along the creek, a sheriff who owes everyone, and a railroad survey that wants the water. The week you ride into Gilead, a homesteader is found hanged at the ford with a sign on him. Everyone knows who did it. Everyone is wrong. Pick a side, or don't, and find out who hanged Owen Lasker before the valley goes to war. Levels 2–6.

synopsis: Bitter Creek runs sixty miles east out of the high country toward the North Platte, a ribbon of willow and cottonwood through a grass valley the size of a small country, and in the spring of 1886 two kinds of people want it. The Bitter Creek Land & Cattle Company, the BC, runs thirty thousand head on the open range with money from the Laramie Club and a syndicate of Edinburgh investors, and claims the whole valley by custom, though it owns hardly an acre of it. Along the creek, on quarter-sections filed under the Homestead Act, live forty families of homesteaders and small ranchers, Norwegians and Missourians, a Black cavalry veteran, a Tejano horse-breaker, a widow doctor, organised into Bitter Creek Grange No. 9 and fencing the water. The Platte River Stock Growers' Association, the big outfits' club in Cheyenne, calls every small man who brands a motherless calf a rustler, and keeps a list. In April a railroad survey party for the Sweetwater & Big Horn Railway is coming up the valley, and wherever it puts its water station and division point, land worth a dollar an acre will be worth a hundred. On the morning of Monday 19 April 1886, Thea Lasker walks down to the ford below her cabin at the Narrows and finds her husband Owen hanging from the big cottonwood with a sign on his chest: RUSTLER. THE ASSOCIATION GIVES FAIR WARNING. Everyone in Ransom County knows who did it: the BC's hired range detective, Jubal Stroud, or the Company's cowboys on his orders. Everyone is wrong. Owen Lasker was hanged by two drifters, Elam Henley and Ira Pettit, paid two hundred dollars by Gideon Sayre, the county's land locator, notary and United States Commissioner, the grange's own secretary, and the man who has been selling the Association its names for the dead list at twenty-five dollars a head. Owen had found out both things Sayre most needed hidden: that he was the informer, and that the railroad's water station will be at the Narrows, on Owen's unproved claim, which Sayre has already taken from the widow with a forged relinquishment. The hanging was dressed up as the Association's to hide the motive and to start a war that would empty the creek of homesteaders and leave their claims for sale cheap. It is working. The party arrives that week, hired by whoever gets to them first. Over eight weeks and four scenarios, the hanging, the spring roundup, the siege of a homestead and the reckoning in town, the Company, the grange, the Association's gunman, the sheriff, the newspaper and the railroad all act on their own clocks. The party can find out who hanged Owen Lasker, keep the widow's claim, stop a massacre at Solberg's Bend and a second hanging in Gilead, face Jubal Stroud in the street, or take somebody's money and look away. The valley will remember what they did.
hook: Gilead, Ransom County, Wyoming Territory, Monday 19 April 1886, a little after noon. The Rawlins stage, or your own horses, come down the last long grade into the Bitter Creek valley with the snow still lying white in the north-facing draws and the creek running high and brown with melt. Gilead is two hundred people, one wide muddy street, the Antelope Saloon, Greaves Mercantile, a brick bank, the two-storey frame Ransom County courthouse that the town is very proud of, and a newspaper office with a hand-lettered bulletin in its window. There is a crowd in front of the window. A boy on a mule came in an hour ago from the Narrows, eleven miles up the creek, with the news: Owen Lasker, homesteader, has been found hanged from the cottonwood at the ford, with a sign on him. The crowd splits along a line you can see. Men in high-heeled boots and big hats on one side of the street, outside the Antelope, saying nothing and looking pleased or sick. Men in brogans and overalls and women in sunbonnets on the other, outside the mercantile, saying the same name over and over: Stroud. By the time you have tied your horses, three different people have tried to hire you. A well-dressed man from the cattle company's office offers range inspectors' wages, sixty dollars a month and found. A grey-haired Norwegian woman, the head of the homesteaders' grange, offers what the grange can raise and a place at every table on the creek. The sheriff, who looks as though he has not slept, offers a deputy's badge at three dollars a day. And at the edge of the crowd, a young woman with a six-year-old boy by the hand and a coffee can under her arm says nothing at all, and looks at you.

setting.name: The Bitter Creek valley and Gilead, Ransom County, Wyoming Territory, 19 April to 12 June 1886
setting.description: Bitter Creek, Gilead and Ransom County are fictional; the territory, the year and the history are real. Wyoming is a territory of sixty thousand people and perhaps two million cattle. The great open-range boom of the early 1880s, when Eastern and British money poured into cattle companies on the promise of free grass, is at its height and about to break: the range is overstocked, beef prices are falling, the summer of 1886 will be dry, and the winter of 1886 to 1887 will kill most of the cattle on the northern plains. Nobody in the valley knows that yet. What they know is that the Homestead Act lets any citizen, or anyone who has declared the intention to become one, file on a hundred and sixty acres, live on it five years and own it, and that the homesteaders have been taking up the creek bottoms, the only water, one quarter-section at a time. The Bitter Creek valley runs east from the foothills of the high country to the sagebrush flats above the North Platte, two days' ride north of the Union Pacific at Rawlins. The upper valley is the Company's: the BC Home Ranch at the Forks, where the creek's two branches meet, with its big log house, its bunkhouses, corrals and a manager from Edinburgh by way of Laramie. The middle valley is the homesteaders': cabins and soddies along the creek every half mile, irrigation ditches, wire fence, Solberg's Bend with the grange hall, and the Narrows, where the valley pinches between two sandstone bluffs, the creek can be forded and dammed, and the railroad's survey says it will put its water tank, roundhouse and division town. Below the Narrows the creek runs out onto the Sage Flats, the Company's spring roundup grounds, and on past Gilead toward the Platte. To the south are the Red Breaks, badland country of clay and cedar where a man can hide a horse herd or himself. Ransom County was carved out of Carbon County by the legislature in 1885, with the Company's money and the homesteaders' votes, and Gilead is its county seat: it has a courthouse, a sheriff, three county commissioners, a justice of the peace, and a U.S. Commissioner who takes homestead filings and final proofs and sends them to the General Land Office at Cheyenne. The valley's people are as mixed as the West was: Norwegian and Swedish homesteaders, Missourians and Ohioans, a Black veteran of the Tenth Cavalry with a hundred head of his own, Tejano and Mexican vaqueros who taught the Company's cowboys their trade, a Chinese-American instrument man with the railroad survey, Irish teamsters, a woman doctor from Philadelphia, Scots bookkeepers and Texas cowhands. They are neighbours, rivals, customers and voters.
setting.atmosphere: Big country and weather. The wind never stops; it comes down the valley from the snowfields in the morning and back up it in the afternoon, smelling of sage, wet earth, woodsmoke and cattle. April is mud and snowmelt and the creek running bank-full; May is grass coming green on the flats, calving, the roundup, and one last spring storm that turns the world white for a day and a night; June is wild roses, mosquitoes on the creek and dust on the road. Distances are long and the GM should make them felt: eleven miles from Gilead to the Narrows is half a morning on a good horse, and a message takes as long as a rider. Sounds: a windmill creaking, a meadowlark, cattle bawling at the roundup, a blacksmith's hammer, the stage driver's horn on the Rawlins road, a rifle shot carrying three miles in still air. The tone is a western paperback: hard men and harder women, bad coffee, good horses, a hanging that the valley cannot stop talking about, a gunfight that lasts four seconds and is remembered for forty years. Lynching is a crime and a horror, never justice. The Company is not a gang of devils and the grange is not a congregation of saints; almost everyone believes they are defending their home, and almost everyone is partly right. Let the land be a character: the creek is the prize, the weather is a faction, and the newspaper prints what the party did, a day late and slanted.

regions.name: Gilead
regions.description: The county seat, two hundred people on a bend of the creek where the Rawlins road crosses it. One wide street of mud or dust. The Ransom County courthouse, two storeys of new frame with a cupola and a jail of two iron cells in the back, where Sheriff Silas Quinlan sleeps more often than at home. The Antelope Saloon, owned two-thirds by Rufus Kemble and one-third, since a poker game in March, by Beaumont Fairchild. Greaves Mercantile, which sells everything and keeps a credit ledger on half the valley. The Gilead Plainsman, a weekly printed on Saturdays on a hand press by Lavinia Thorpe. The bank, the livery and smithy, a two-storey hotel called the Ransom House, Dr. Abigail Haskell's surgery, a Methodist chapel without a minister, and, in a neat little office beside the courthouse with a gilt-lettered window, Gideon Sayre: Land Locator, Notary Public, U.S. Commissioner.

regions.name: The Upper Valley and the Forks
regions.description: The Company's country. The BC Home Ranch sits where the north and south branches of Bitter Creek meet: a two-storey log house with a glassed veranda, a piano and a manager, Cyrus Ballantine; three bunkhouses, a cookhouse, a blacksmith shop, a commissary, horse corrals and a remuda of four hundred horses. Range boss Wade Tolliver runs forty riders out of it in the season. Line camps are scattered up both branches, and the Company's winter hay is stacked at the Sage Flats camp. The Company owns the Forks and a few dozen quarter-sections its own cowboys filed on and signed over; the rest it holds by custom, by force, and by the fact that it got here first.

regions.name: The Middle Creek: Solberg's Bend and the Narrows
regions.description: The homesteaders' country, twenty miles of creek bottom with a claim every half mile: log cabins and sod houses, potato patches, irrigation ditches, milk cows, small herds of a few dozen head under their own brands, and barbed wire that the Company's riders cut and the homesteaders mend. Solberg's Bend is the biggest and oldest place, Margit Solberg's homestead, with a frame house, a stone root cellar, hay barns and the log grange hall where Bitter Creek Grange No. 9 meets on Saturday nights. Eight miles upstream the valley pinches at the Narrows between two red sandstone bluffs: the best ford on the creek, a natural dam site, the big cottonwood, and Owen and Thea Lasker's one-room cabin. Calvin Booker's ranch is in Booker's Draw, a side valley with a spring, south of the Bend.

regions.name: The Sage Flats and the Red Breaks
regions.description: Below the Narrows the valley opens into the Sage Flats, miles of sagebrush and spring grass where the Association's general roundup gathers every May, the Company's hay is stacked at its line camp, and the Sweetwater & Big Horn survey party pitches its tents. South of the creek the land breaks up into the Red Breaks, a maze of clay gullies, cedar, hidden springs and box canyons, where rustlers, real ones, hold stolen horses until they can be run south to Colorado, and where Fergus Mallory has a cabin no one else can find.

campaignRules.name: The Range War Clock
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on a calendar from Monday 19 April to Saturday 12 June 1886, and every faction acts on it whether or not the players are watching. bk-scenario-001 is the week of the hanging (19 to 24 April); bk-scenario-002 the spring roundup (10 to 22 May); bk-scenario-003 the siege of Solberg's Bend (24 to 27 May); bk-scenario-004 the reckoning in Gilead (5 to 12 June). Between scenarios, the GM summarises the weeks that pass and lets the players choose one or two things to do. Track the date openly. If the players do not interfere, this happens. THE COMPANY: on Friday 23 April eight hired gunmen from Cheyenne arrive on the Rawlins stage with Association 'stock inspector' commissions; Jubal Stroud nails thirty-day warnings on Nils Solberg's door and Fergus Mallory's empty cabin (Calvin Booker's went up on Saturday 17 April, the day before the hanging, and Joe Pruneda's on 20 April); on Saturday 24 April Cyrus Ballantine offers Thea Lasker $300 for the Narrows and is refused; in the roundup (10 to 22 May) the Company claims every maverick and drives homesteaders' strays into its herd; on 13 May Stroud's men ambush Calvin Booker's rider, Joe Pruneda, and wound him; on 24 May the thirty days run out and a Rawlins justice of the peace, paid by the Company, issues warrants for 'cattle theft' against the dead-list men; at dawn on Wednesday 26 May Ballantine, Stroud, the Association gunmen and eight Company riders, sixteen guns, surround Solberg's Bend. THE GRANGE: the funeral is Wednesday 21 April; the grange meets Saturday 24 April, votes to arm, and sends Margit Solberg to Cheyenne to petition the territorial governor (she is gone until 8 May); after the ambush on Booker's rider, Nils Solberg and four young men burn the Company's hay at the Sage Flats camp on the night of 17 May; on the night of 25 May the dead-list men and their families gather at Solberg's Bend for safety, which is what Ballantine is counting on. GIDEON SAYRE: on Tuesday 20 April he records Elam Henley's homestead entry on the Narrows quarter on the strength of Owen Lasker's forged relinquishment, and mails both to Cheyenne on 22 April; at the grange meeting on 24 April he speaks hardest for arming; on the night of the blizzard, 15 May, Henley kills Ira Pettit, who has been talking, and leaves him in the path of the stampede; on 26 May Sayre sends Henley with the Company's raiders, as a hired gun, to shoot Thea Lasker at Solberg's Bend in the confusion; on Monday 7 June the railroad's land agent arrives and Sayre, through Henley, sells him the Narrows for $6,000; Sayre means to leave on the Tuesday 8 June stage. THE RAILROAD: the survey party reaches the Sage Flats on 12 May and stakes the line up the creek to the Narrows by 20 May; on 7 June its land agent, Prosper Gault, presents the right-of-way petition to the county commissioners at a public meeting in the courthouse. THE LAW: Sheriff Quinlan does nothing he can avoid; he serves the Company's warrants on 25 May unless someone gives him a reason not to; Judge Amasa Kittle opens the district court term in Gilead on Monday 7 June. Whatever the players change, the people they have not touched carry on, adapting only to what they could plausibly know.

campaignRules.name: Reputation on Bitter Creek
campaignRules.description: Use frontier.json's Reputation rules: the party has one Reputation score in Gilead and the valley, from -5 to +5, tracked openly and announced when it changes. It starts at 0: strangers. It rises for fair dealing in public, protecting someone who cannot protect themselves, standing up in a showdown and walking away clean, keeping your word to either side, and finding out the truth and saying it. It falls for bullying, cheating at cards, shooting an unarmed or surrendering man, backing down from a fair challenge, breaking your word, and taking part in or standing by at a hanging. Separately, the GM tracks two attitudes, the Company's and the grange's, as hostile, wary, neutral, friendly or trusting; they move with what the party does for or against each side, and a party that works for one side starts wary with the other. At Reputation +3, Greaves gives credit, the Plainsman prints your side, and both factions will at least meet you. At +5 the town will stand behind you in the street. At -3 nobody rents you a room or sells you cartridges, and the Company or the grange (whichever you have hurt) puts your names on a list of its own. At -5 a mob or a posse comes for you.

campaignRules.name: Who Hanged Owen Lasker
campaignRules.description: The mystery inside the war, run on the three-clue rule. Every conclusion the players need has at least three clues in different places, named in the control file (lettered A to F) and in each scenario; core clues are found by anyone who looks in the right place with the right skill, without a roll; rolls add detail, speed or safety, and a failed roll costs time, a horse, Reputation or a faction's goodwill, never the truth. The war is loud and the mystery is quiet: the GM should let the players feel that every faction wants them busy with the shooting. If the table is stuck, have a companion lay the case out by lamplight: what the sign was written on, whose horse wore the bar shoe, who has been spending money, who filed on the Narrows, and who gains if the creek empties.

campaignRules.name: The Dead List
campaignRules.description: The Platte River Stock Growers' Association keeps a list of men on Bitter Creek it calls rustlers. In April it has ten names: Owen Lasker (struck through), Calvin Booker, Fergus Mallory, Nils Solberg, Joe Pruneda, the Kettleson brothers, young Wiley Dorsett, Lars Engstrom, and 'the Swede preacher' (Gustav Lindahl, if he is played; otherwise a homesteader named Per Aaberg). Stroud's method is fixed and he is proud of it: a thirty-day warning on a cartridge-box card nailed to the door, then a warrant or a bullet. A name can be added: a party that sides openly with the grange, or kills a Company man, should expect a card on its own door. Use frontier.json's Wanted levels for any warrant that follows: the Company can get local warrants from the bought justice in Rawlins; killing a lawman or a Company man in front of witnesses makes it territorial; dead or alive needs a judge, and Judge Kittle will not sign one without evidence. The list is evidence too: the Association's copy is annotated with where each name came from.

campaignRules.name: Showdowns, Horses and the Trail
campaignRules.description: Use frontier.json for showdowns, horses, the trail and weather. Jubal Stroud will only fight a man face to face, in daylight, with witnesses, and he will offer a showdown to any party member who shames him; the stare-down is real and backing down costs Reputation. A fair fight in front of the town raises Reputation for the winner; a shot from cover, a second gun, or killing a man who has dropped his pistol lowers it by 2. Distances by horse on the valley roads: Gilead to Solberg's Bend 9 miles, to the Narrows 11 miles, to Booker's Draw 12 miles, to the Forks 28 miles, to the Sage Flats roundup camp 6 miles; Gilead to Rawlins and the railroad 54 miles, two days by stage (Tuesday and Friday, $6) or a day and a half hard riding. The nearest telegraph is at Rawlins. A good horse is part of a character: name it, and if it dies, it matters. Weather is a faction: April mud halves travel off the roads, the 15 May blizzard closes the valley for a day and a night, and June dust shows a rider at five miles.

explorationRules: This is a valley sandbox and the map is a schematic of it: the Company's Forks at the head of the creek in the west, the homesteaders' middle creek with Solberg's Bend and the Narrows, the Sage Flats and the survey camp below, Gilead on the Rawlins road to the east, the Red Breaks to the south. The party moves on horseback, by buckboard or on the Tuesday and Friday stage, and the unit of time is the half-day. The Range War Clock (campaignRules) is the engine: every half-day spent somewhere is a half-day not spent somewhere else, and the factions keep moving. In session one the players choose who hires them, the Company, the grange, the sheriff, or the widow Thea Lasker; each pregen's sheet suggests one, and a party may split its loyalties, which is fine and dramatic. Run each scenario as a set of named places listed in it, with each faction acting on its schedule and on what it could know. Nobody is omniscient: Ballantine knows what Tolliver, Stroud and the Association gunmen tell him; the grange knows what its members see and what Sayre, its secretary, chooses to report; Sayre knows a great deal, because everyone tells the notary everything. The mystery follows the three-clue rule (campaignRules); fights are short, loud and consequential, and most scenes are a conversation across a kitchen table, a corral rail or a poker hand with someone who wants something. Between scenes let the land breathe: a meadowlark on a fence post, a band of antelope watching from a ridge, calves bawling, a windmill, snowmelt in the creek, the stage horn on the Rawlins road. Money is 1886 dollars: a cowhand earns $40 a month and found, a good horse costs $60, a quarter-section's improvements sell for $300, and the railroad will pay $6,000 for the Narrows. The players should come away knowing what Bitter Creek looked like, and feeling that whatever they chose, it cost something.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a character's hit points, it does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Bitter Creek, Gilead, Ransom County, the Bitter Creek Land & Cattle Company, the Platte River Stock Growers' Association, the Sweetwater & Big Horn Railway and every person in the campaign are fictional. Wyoming Territory, 1886, the Homestead Act, the General Land Office at Cheyenne, the open-range cattle boom, the general roundup, the stock associations and their blacklists, and the conflicts between big cattle outfits and homesteaders are real history; this is an analogue of those conflicts, not a retelling of any one, and no real person appears.
controlFile.theTruth: Owen Lasker, thirty-one, came to the creek from Iowa in 1883 and filed on the Narrows quarter-section; he has not yet lived there the five years needed to prove up. Short of cash, he spent the winter of 1885 to 1886 working as a chainman for the Sweetwater & Big Horn Railway's survey party in the foothills, and in March, copying a profile for the chief engineer, he saw that the railroad means to put its water station, roundhouse and division town at the Narrows, where the creek can be dammed. On 2 April, filing a brand registration at Gideon Sayre's office in Gilead, Owen saw on Sayre's desk a letter from the Association's secretary in Cheyenne thanking 'G.S.' for 'the names received' and enclosing $75: three names at $25 a head. Owen's was one of them. Sayre, the valley's land locator, notary public and U.S. Commissioner, and the grange's founding secretary, has been the Association's informer since 1884, and has also been buying up the claims of homesteaders who are frightened off, through dummy entrymen, against the day the railroad comes. On Friday 16 April Owen, who was brave and not careful, walked into Sayre's office and told him he knew, that he would say so at the grange meeting on Saturday 24 April, and that he would sell the Narrows to the railroad himself. Sayre hired two drifters he had used before as dummy entrymen, Elam Henley and Ira Pettit, ex-BC riders whom Wade Tolliver fired in February for drinking: $100 each in advance and $200 each after, and Henley would file on the Narrows and sign it over to Sayre. On Saturday 17 April Pettit bought forty feet of new manila rope at Greaves Mercantile. Sayre lettered the sign himself, RUSTLER. THE ASSOCIATION GIVES FAIR WARNING, in his neat copperplate on the back of the only stiff paper to hand, a blank General Land Office form, and forged a relinquishment of Owen's entry dated 10 April, with Henley and Pettit as witnesses. On the night of Sunday 18 April Henley and Pettit called Owen out of his cabin to help with 'a cow down in the creek', took him at gunpoint to the cottonwood and hanged him. Thea heard horses and thought it was the Company's riders; she did not go out until dawn. The hanging was dressed as the Association's work for two reasons: to hide Sayre's motive, and to start a war that would frighten the homesteaders off the creek and leave their claims for him to buy cheap before the railroad's survey becomes public. Sayre gains whoever wins the war. The Company did not hang Owen Lasker. It is not innocent. The dead list is real, Jubal Stroud has killed two men on it in other valleys, and Cyrus Ballantine means to 'clear the creek' after the roundup with warrants from a bought justice and sixteen guns; the hanging suits him, and he lets the valley believe it was his.
suspects: Gideon Sayre, 49, U.S. Commissioner, land locator, notary public and grange secretary: the man who ordered the hanging. Motive: Owen knew he was the Association's informer and was going to say so, and Owen's death and the forged relinquishment give Sayre the Narrows, worth $6,000 to the railroad. Plan: keep the war going, use Henley to remove Thea Lasker (the widow's right to continue the claim is the only flaw in his title), sell the Narrows on 7 June and leave on the 8 June stage. THIS IS WHAT SUCCEEDS IF NOBODY INTERFERES.

Elam Henley, 34, drifter, ex-BC rider: one of the two hangmen, and the dangerous one. Rides a bay with a bar shoe on the near fore. He is the entryman on the Narrows on paper. He killed Pettit in the blizzard and will try for Thea at the siege.

Ira Pettit, 20, drifter, ex-BC rider: the other hangman, who bought the rope. Sick with it, drinking, talking. If the party reaches him before 15 May and protects him, he confesses. If not, he dies in the stampede on the night of the blizzard.

Jubal Stroud, 40, the Association's range detective on the Company's payroll: the man everyone blames. Motive enough: Owen was on his list. He did not do it, and he is insulted that anyone thinks he would hang a man before his thirty days were up, or with a sign like a schoolboy's. He is a killer by trade and proud of his rules.

Cyrus Ballantine, 51, manager of the Bitter Creek Land & Cattle Company: wants the creek cleared of homesteaders and the Narrows in the Company's hands before the railroad comes. He did not order the hanging, but he lets it frighten the valley, offers the widow $300, and plans the raid on Solberg's Bend.

Nils Solberg, 24, Margit's son, on the dead list: hot-headed and grieving for his friend Owen. The grange's most likely man to do something terrible in return. He burns the Company's hay and, in the finale, leads the mob that wants to hang Henley.
redHerrings: Jubal Stroud. Everything points at him at first: the sign names the Association, Owen was on his list, and he was seen on the creek road on the Saturday. He was there to nail his warning on Calvin Booker's door. Played straight, he becomes the party's strangest witness: he will tell them, with professional contempt, exactly why the hanging was not his work.

Cyrus Ballantine's $300 offer for the Narrows, and the letter in Owen's cabin from the Company offering $1,500 for it in February, make it look as though the Company killed him when he refused to sell. The Company wanted the Narrows; it was negotiating, not killing.

Fergus Mallory, the valley's actual rustler, was seen near the Narrows on Sunday night with a band of horses. He was moving stolen Company horses into the Red Breaks, saw two riders on the creek road by moonlight, and will say so if he trusts the party. He is a witness, not a suspect, but a party working for the Company may want to hang him for it.

Owen's grange friends whisper that Owen was 'selling out' to the Company or the railroad, and a few wonder if a neighbour did it. Owen was going to sell to the railroad, for the creek's sake as well as his own: his letter to the chief engineer asks that the dam leave water for the ditches below.
clues: A. THE HANGING WAS NOT THE ASSOCIATION'S OR THE COMPANY'S WORK. A1: the sign is neat copperplate in black ink on the back of a printed General Land Office blank, not Stroud's crude pencil (bk-scenario-001). A2: Stroud's real warning, a cartridge-box card dated 5 April giving Owen thirty days, still nailed inside the cabin door where Thea put it; the thirty days had not run (bk-scenario-001). A3: the tracks: two shod horses, one with a bar shoe on the near fore, came from and went back toward Gilead, not the Forks (bk-scenario-001). A4: every Company rider was at the Forks on Sunday night breaking horses, by the cook's tally and Tolliver's word (bk-scenario-001 or 002). A5: Stroud himself, contemptuously: 'I give thirty days. I don't use signs and I don't use rope' (bk-scenario-001 to 003).

B. ELAM HENLEY AND IRA PETTIT DID THE HANGING. B1: the Gilead blacksmith put a bar shoe on Elam Henley's bay in March (bk-scenario-001). B2: Greaves Mercantile's ledger: forty feet of new 3/4-inch manila sold to Ira Pettit on Saturday 17 April, paid in cash, though Pettit owes the store $11 (bk-scenario-001). B3: Henley and Pettit paid off $100 of debts each at the Antelope and the livery that week, in new banknotes (bk-scenario-001 or 002). B4: Pettit, drunk at the roundup: 'It takes so long. Nobody tells you it takes so long' (bk-scenario-002). B5: Henley's homestead entry on the Narrows quarter, dated 20 April, in Sayre's commissioner's register (bk-scenario-002 or 004). B6: Pettit's confession if he lives, or Henley's if taken alive (bk-scenario-002 to 004).

C. GIDEON SAYRE PAID FOR IT. C1: Sayre's copperplate hand and his black ink, on every filing in the county, match the sign; and only the U.S. Commissioner keeps blank Land Office forms (bk-scenario-001 or 002). C2: the forged relinquishment of Owen's entry, dated 10 April and witnessed by Henley and Pettit, when the survey party's payroll book shows Owen working forty miles away in the foothills from 6 to 13 April (bk-scenario-002). C3: the Association's annotated dead list, taken from Stroud's saddlebag or Ballantine's desk: beside six of the ten names, 'per G.S., Gilead' (bk-scenario-003). C4: Owen's notebook, hidden in the family Bible: 'G.S. is the one giving names. Saw the letter. Told him. Will say it at grange Sat. 24th' (bk-scenario-001 or 002, from Thea once she trusts the party). C5: Sayre's letter of 20 March to the railroad's land department offering 'the Narrows quarter, title to be clear by June', in the hands of the land agent, Prosper Gault (bk-scenario-004). C6: Pettit's or Henley's word that 'the notary' paid them (bk-scenario-002 to 004).

D. THE COMPANY MEANS TO CLEAR THE CREEK. D1: the dead list and Stroud's thirty-day cards on the doors (bk-scenario-001). D2: eight hired gunmen with Association commissions arrive on 23 April (bk-scenario-001). D3: Ballantine's telegram, copied by the Rawlins operator or seen on his desk: 'WILL CLEAR CREEK AFTER ROUNDUP STOP NEED PAPERS FROM RAWLINS STOP' (bk-scenario-002). D4: Wade Tolliver, if he is turned, tells the party the date of the raid (bk-scenario-002 or 003). D5: the Rawlins warrants, sworn 24 May (bk-scenario-003).

E. THE NARROWS IS THE PRIZE. E1: the survey profile, which Henry Lau or chief engineer Horace Wendt can show the party: water station, dam and division point at the Narrows (bk-scenario-002). E2: Owen's draft letter to Wendt, asking that the dam leave water for the ditches below (bk-scenario-001 or 002). E3: Ballantine's offers, $1,500 in February and $300 to the widow (bk-scenario-001). E4: Prosper Gault's draft for $6,000 and his right-of-way petition (bk-scenario-004).

F. HENLEY RIDES WITH THE RAIDERS TO KILL THEA LASKER. F1: Henley is not on the Company's payroll but rides with the Association gunmen on 26 May; Tolliver does not know who hired him (bk-scenario-003). F2: during the siege he works round to the house's blind side, where Thea and the children are, not toward the fight (bk-scenario-003). F3: a widow continuing her husband's claim defeats a relinquishment she can prove was forged; Judge Kittle or Lavinia Thorpe can explain it, and so can Thea (bk-scenario-002 to 004).
controlFile.theKeyClue: The players solve the mystery when they stop asking who hates the homesteaders and start asking who gains from the Narrows. Everything turns on the sign: it was written on Land Office paper in a clerk's hand. Point the first scenario's clues (A and B) hard, and let the sign be the thing a companion keeps coming back to. If the party reaches the roundup without suspecting anyone but Stroud, have Stroud himself ride up to their fire and tell them, with contempt, that he has never in his life used a sign.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no single right ending, only consequences. OWEN LASKER'S KILLERS: Sayre is untouchable by gossip; he is a federal officer and the grange's own secretary. He falls only on evidence that reaches Judge Kittle: the forged relinquishment against the survey payroll, plus Pettit's confession or Henley's, or the annotated dead list, or Gault's letter. Then he is indicted, the forged papers are void, and he hangs by law in the autumn, or the party lets the mob have him, which is a hanging all the same. THEA LASKER: if she survives the siege and the forgery is proved, her claim stands and she sells the Narrows to the railroad herself, on terms that leave water for the ditches below; the creek gets its town. If she dies, the Narrows goes to Henley's title, Sayre and the railroad. THE WAR: if the raid on Solberg's Bend succeeds, homesteaders die, the rest leave, and the Company holds the creek; if it is stopped by force, the Company is broken in the courts and the grange holds the creek; if Tolliver is turned and the truth about the hanging is out before 26 May, the raid can be called off and the two sides can be brought to the courthouse to divide the water, which is the hardest ending and the best. JUBAL STROUD: he can be faced in the street, outwitted, exposed in the Plainsman, or simply outlived; the Association recalls him if the dead list is printed. THE EPILOGUE: whatever happens, the winter of 1886 to 1887 is coming, the worst the northern range will ever see. The GM should end the campaign with the first snow in October and a line about which ranches had hay put up, and which did not.
